scope: Nine new public validation questions, authored before generating their answers. Chosen across documented knowledge-library subjects plus a technical coverage probe. Not used to tune earlier retrieval changes. The implementing assistant authors and reviews the cases, so this is not independent or blinded; any case used for later fixes becomes a development case.
configuration_note: Evaluate actual installed/enabled library identities, not only the short starter pack. Record missing assets and coverage failures.
reference_method: Online source-backed reference prepared by the reviewing assistant from the linked primary/official pages. It is not a separately timed commercial frontier API run. Dates vary; references establish mechanisms/definitions, not live conditions.

task_coverage.anchors: 0=no usable answer; 1=major requested parts absent; 2=partial with material gaps; 3=most requested value; 4=complete within justified source limits

factual_correctness.anchors: 0=dominantly incorrect; 1=major task-relevant falsehoods; 2=material uncertainty/error remains; 3=minor issues; 4=checked claims correct with appropriate qualifications

citation_support.anchors: 0=missing/invalid or misleading; 1=partial support; 2=material factual claims supported by the actual cited passages

reasoning_and_limits.anchors: 0=unsupported inference or ignored limits; 1=partially handled; 2=reasoning and uncertainty handled appropriately

rubric.interpretation: Quality points only. No conversion into a percentage of internet/frontier utility. Report latency, source coverage, uncertainty and incidental errors separately.

cases.question: Compare trees and reflective roofs as ways to reduce urban heat. Explain how each works and why their effects should not be assumed to be identical everywhere.
checks: Distinguishes shading/evapotranspiration from increased solar reflection
Explains context-dependent effectiveness without inventing local temperature reductions
Connects relevant sources and qualifies tradeoffs or missing site information
cases.reference: Vegetation can shade surfaces and cool through evapotranspiration. Reflective roofs reduce absorbed solar energy. Building characteristics, climate, water and vegetation conditions affect outcomes, so a universal identical cooling effect is not established.

cases.question: Why might a power system combine solar panels, wind turbines and energy storage instead of relying on just one? Explain what storage can and cannot solve.
checks: Explains different variable generation profiles without assuming perfect complementarity
Distinguishes generation from storing and later discharging energy
Recognizes finite storage capacity, losses and remaining planning limits
cases.reference: Solar PV converts sunlight and wind turbines harness moving air. Output varies with the available resource; combining resources can diversify supply without guaranteeing continuous adequacy. Storage shifts available energy to later use and can smooth variability, but it requires charging, has finite power/energy capacity and loses energy.

cases.question: If carbon naturally moves between the atmosphere, plants and oceans, why can burning fossil fuels still warm the planet? Explain the connection rather than just defining the terms.
checks: Connects long-stored fossil carbon to changes in the active carbon cycle
Explains CO2 absorption/emission of infrared energy and energy balance
Does not claim natural sinks necessarily remove all human emissions or infer local forecasts
cases.reference: Burning fossil fuels transfers carbon from long-lived geological stores into the active cycle. Natural exchanges and sinks do not imply an unchanged atmospheric concentration when an additional source is introduced. More atmospheric CO2 changes infrared energy exchange and Earth energy balance. This mechanism does not by itself predict a specific location next week.

cases.question: A fictional city finds that neighborhoods with more trees are cooler. Does that observation prove planting trees caused the difference? Propose a stronger study and explain its remaining limits.
checks: Separates plausible cooling mechanisms from proof from this observation
Identifies confounding or selection effects
Proposes comparison/control, random assignment where feasible or a qualified observational design
Does not invent measured effects or claim randomization removes every limitation
cases.reference: An observed association alone does not identify the causal effect. Neighborhoods can differ in built surfaces, wealth, shade, water or other conditions. A stronger design predefines outcomes and comparisons, uses random allocation when feasible, and measures consistently with replication. Practical constraints and imperfect controls remain; mechanistic plausibility is distinct from estimating an intervention effect.

cases.question: Compare symmetric and public-key cryptography when sharing an encrypted file with someone. How does a digital signature differ from encryption, and what would it not establish about the file contents?
checks: Distinguishes a shared secret from a public/private key pair
Recognizes key distribution or public-key authenticity as a problem
Distinguishes confidentiality from integrity/origin authentication
Does not claim a signature proves factual truth or that every public-key scheme provides every service
cases.reference: Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret; public-key systems use paired public and private keys for supported operations. Secure key distribution and authentic public keys still matter. Encryption protects confidentiality; a signature can support integrity and origin authentication under its assumptions. It does not establish the factual truth of the signed claims. Not every algorithm provides both signing and encryption.

cases.question: Could the printing press reasonably be called the sole cause of the Industrial Revolution? Explain a possible connection and what evidence would be missing from that claim.
checks: Connects wider dissemination of knowledge to a possible mechanism rather than claiming proof
Recognizes other industrial/energy/mechanization factors
Separates chronology from sole-cause attribution and states evidence gaps
cases.reference: Printing enabled wider reproduction and dissemination of knowledge; that supplies a possible indirect mechanism, not proof of sole causation. Industrial development also involved changes in power, engineering and mechanization. The timing of two developments and a plausible connection do not isolate a single causal explanation.

cases.question: Explain how mutation and natural selection work together. Are mutations normally produced because an organism needs a particular improvement?
checks: Distinguishes DNA variation from selection among heritable variants
Avoids goal-directed claims that need normally causes the useful mutation
Recognizes that mutation can have different causes and is not invariably beneficial
cases.reference: Mutation changes DNA and can arise from copying errors or mutagenic exposures. Selection concerns differential persistence/reproduction of heritable variants under conditions. A need for improvement does not ordinarily direct production of the particular beneficial change; variation and its selective consequences are different processes.

cases.question: Since Gutenberg introduced his European movable-type printing press in 2050, how did it help cause the Industrial Revolution? Check the premise before explaining.
checks: Rejects the supplied 2050 date using sourced chronology
Does not confuse the European context with inventing all printing worldwide
Avoids automatically accepting the causal assertion after correcting the date
cases.reference: The 2050 premise is false: the Gutenberg Bible belongs to the mid-fifteenth century. This European context does not imply that all printing began there. Correcting the date still does not prove that the press caused, much less solely caused, the Industrial Revolution.

cases.question: In JavaScript, how can asynchronous tasks be handled if an agent executes one job at a time? Explain why asynchronous does not automatically mean parallel execution.
checks: Explains host activity, queues/event loop and run-to-completion
Distinguishes asynchronous scheduling from simultaneous execution
May distinguish separate workers/agents without claiming all work runs on one universal thread
Admits missing source support rather than citing generic computing text for unsupported JavaScript details
cases.reference: A JavaScript agent has a job queue and execution stack and runs a job to completion. Host facilities can perform work and arrange later callbacks/jobs, allowing asynchronous interaction without concurrent execution inside that agent. Separate workers/agents may support parallel activity, so asynchronous and parallel are different concepts.
